Transactions do, calls dont. 🙂 <@689161464829050960> I recommend following RFC 2119 for word choices, which means `**MUST**` instead of `shall`. Sure, I can do that. I am new around here, but I have been involved in a number of protocol discussions to do with networking etc, I think using the RFC structure for EIP's wouldn't be the worst you know sorry if that is off topic No worries! Probably the best place to discuss would be <#746566142700814426> ? Welcome to the party 🎉 <@689161464829050960> I feel like the call arguments are in the wrong order? It says `top-0` is the "most recently pushed item on the stack", but I believe that the order is effectively opposite for the other call opcodes? Where `retLength` is the last thing pushed on the stack before the call. (I may be wrong here, been a bit since I have looked at the EVM that closely and <@161241965181140994> could probably give an immediate answer) https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/blob/44c0bb2b44ca71790ccf8a842eccaa72619a2a02/core/vm/instructions.go#L642 I've done quite a bit of calling in my day 😉 gas is the most recent, then addr, value, inOffset, etc Huh. TIL. I had to double check myself, which is why I had the link handy 😉 I _think_ EIP-3074 is shaping up nicely. I might be biased though I'm hoping we can get it into Review soon to increase its chances of London inclusion. Recommend removing the extraneous `valid` here: Same for `success` below it. Or turn them into `#####` headings. https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/blame/master/EIPS/eip-3074.md#L114 I think they already are Just doesn't render well Ah, yeah. If they have the \`...\` around them then that style overrides the heading style. It doesn't always though :\ In this case, I would probably remove the code block (though I can appreciate why you have it there). I just wanted monospace headings 😛 Yeah, I would have defaulted to the same thing as you I think. Maybe change the heading to something like this? ``` Return Value - `valid` Return Value - `success` ``` Just to help make it more clear when rendered that it is a heading line? Sure! Is the idea with removing `gas` from the check that a user should verify that the sponsor contract does the right thing before using it, so we don't have to sign over it? Yeppers Why not also include `chainId` in `extra` then (for the same reason)? Yeah... I think it can go as well. It just feels like checking chain id is the common case Where gas... maybe not so much with trusted sponsors? Do we gain something significant by trying to guess and then optimize the common case here? The tiniest of gas savings, and a tiny bit less complexity in the invoker? Having more explicit checks in the invoker rather than implicit checks by `CALLFROM` may lend itself to auditability/readability. The gas savings should be on the order of less than 1 I would imagine? like 15 or so We still have to look up and check the `chainid` in either case, putting the check inside the opcode just means we don't have to do gas accounting between operations. Yeah, I'll take it out <@!543900561460822016>'s been pushing to remove `type` as well, and just stick a double zero at the start of the signed bytes. You mean change `SPONSORED_TYPE` to `0x0`? No, use 0x00 0x00 That would be `SPONSORED_TYPE` `0x0`. It would just be a magic 2byte uint16 vs uint8 I think That is, it would consume the signature space for type `0`. Idk what serialization scheme would start with a 0x00? Anything after the first byte can be whatever we want. What matters is that it is consuming the transaction type 0 signature space. I know RLP wouldn’t, maybe SSZ would? I’d be happy if we came up with something that wouldn’t collide with those two The idea with typed transactions is that we shouldn't have to *ever* worry about signature collision between transaction types. That is, when developing a new transaction type, no one should have to think harder than "is my first byte unique". RLP today, SSZ tomorrow, something else after that, raw message signing after that, etc. Nothing should ever possibly collide as long as you follow the **one** simple rule of "unique first byte". In hindsight, the name `Transaction Type` is a misnomer, it should be `Signature Type`. "Envelope" 🤔 I wonder if it is too late to rename it... Don't let your dreams be dreams! "Signed Data Envelope Type" Nah, we haven’t shipped it yet Easy fix Unfortunately 2718 actually includes more than just that, it also specifies merkle trie encoding, receipt encoding, etc. 😢 Apparently I failed at following my own rule of "don't confound concerns in EIPs"! Sorry to change the topic, but I am somewhat worried about the whole `tx.origin == msg.sender` thing. The safest option is still to ban self-sponsoring. What are you worried about? Anyone who ever uses that check for any reason lol There *will* be contracts that break. We (security community) have been telling people to **not** do those checks for half a decade. I think at some point, people need to take responsibility for not listening, and for me this crosses that threshold. ~~Actually, what would break exactly <@689161464829050960>?~~ * `tx.origin == me` * `tx.to == my contract` * my contract then conditionally calls external contract * `msg.sender == me` * external contract does `require(tx.origin == msg.sender)` which passes Such defenses were already broken since miners could conditionally call a contract anyway. And this includes MEV Geth, which allows any bot author to conditionally call contracts. To put it another way, I don't believe we are breaking anything that wasn't already broken. If you had an ERC-721 guarded by `require(tx.origin == msg.sender)`, and you called back into it during an `onERC720Received` callback As an example Does that pattern exist in the wild (reentrancy protection via origin check)? No idea I was going to look, but am lazy. Is there a giant database of deployed contracts I can just... grep? 😉 🤷 Same Wouldn't be too hard to check, I think. Just search for ORIGIN in compiled bytecode. I don't think it's super common. Or even contracts containing both ORIGIN and SENDER. Finding all contracts with `require(tx.origin == msg.sender)` wouldn't be hard. Figuring out *why* they are using it is harder. Agreed There are a lot of contracts that mistakenly think `require(tx.origin == msg.sender)` protects them from conditional execution. Like gambling games, for example. Yeah, I noted that in the security section. This certainly makes conditional execution easier lol <@!187490121698770945> What are your thoughts of putting a "list" into eth1.0-specs for the various transaction types? We need to make sure they never collide, which means we need to track which ones are "used". We have legacy transactions (which I think consume two types), 2930, 1559, and now 3074. It is eventually going to be hard to track down all of the "used" types, and EIPs aren't a great place for lists that change with time. Huh, "shall" and "required" are also valid RFC2119 <@301186049323958275> FYI https://twitter.com/ricmoo/status/1369378019949809668?s=21 Would <@!543900561460822016>, <@!415548822983278593> or <@!301186049323958275> object to being added as authors on 3074? You've all contributed more than enough to get some credit. No objection

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: There *will* be contracts that break.  We (security community) have been telling people to **not** do those checks for half a decade.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: I think at some point, people need to take responsibility for not listening, and for me this crosses that threshold.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: ~~Actually, what would break exactly <@689161464829050960>?~~

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
* `tx.origin == me`
* `tx.to == my contract`
* my contract then conditionally calls external contract
* `msg.sender == me`
* external contract does `require(tx.origin == msg.sender)` which passes

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Such defenses were already broken since miners could conditionally call a contract anyway.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: And this includes MEV Geth, which allows any bot author to conditionally call contracts.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: To put it another way, I don't believe we are breaking anything that wasn't already broken.

We need to make sure they never collide, which means we need to track which ones are "used".  We have legacy transactions (which I think consume two types), 2930, 1559, and now 3074.
